title: SCHOUTEN v HEALTH NEW ZEALAND
text:
IN THE EMPLOYMENT RELATIONS AUTHORITY
WELLINGTON
I TE RATONGA AHUMANA TAIMAHI
TE WHANGANUI-A-TARA ROHE
[2026] NZERA 520
3391424
BETWEEN FRANCISCUS SCHOUTEN
Applicant
AND HEALTH NEW ZEALAND
Respondent
Member of Authority: Claire English
Representatives: Franciscus Schouten, in Person
Maria Green, counsel for the Respondent
Investigation Meeting: On the Papers
Submissions received: Up to 26 June 2026 from Applicant
6 May 2026 from Respondent
Determination: 04 August 2026
DETERMINATION OF THE AUTHORITY
Employment Relationship Problem
[1] The applicant, Mr Franciscus Schouten, worked as a security guard and orderly
for the respondent, Health New Zealand (HNZ). He was dismissed on 7 November
2022. He now seeks to pursue a claim of unjustified dismissal, and filed a statement of
problem in the Authority on 11 July 2025.
[2] HNZ says that that it has no record of Mr Schouten raising a personal grievance
claim in relation to his dismissal prior to the statement of problem. It does not consent
to any such claim being raised out of time.

[3] Mr Schouten says that he raised a personal grievance claim for unjustified
dismissal on 7 July 2025. He further says that he contacted an employment advocate a
week before his dismissal. He says that the advocate got in contact with him some two-
and-a-half months later, and advised him that he would not be able to take his case. So
he took no action. Mr Schouten also says that he met with a new union representative
in October 2022 to meet them on the resignation of the prior union representative, and
after this, he ceased to pay his union fees for cost-of-living reasons, and his union did
not assist him. He did not give specific dates for when these actions occurred.
[4] He now seeks that the Authority allow him to pursue his personal grievance
claim out of time, on the grounds that exceptional circumstances exist. He says that his
exceptional circumstances are that “I placed my trust in the advocate, only to be
mislead”. He also says he was suffering from trauma and humiliation at the time.
[5] HNZ says that Mr Schouten’s circumstances do not fit within the definition of
exceptional circumstances as set out in section 115 of the Employment Relations Act
2000 (the Act). It says that even on Mr Schouten’s own account, he never hired an
advocate or became a client of an advocate, and he never instructed either the advocate
or his union to raise a grievance on his behalf. HNZ says that the sending of a single
inquiry email to an inbox is simply not enough for Mr Schouten to demonstrate that he
made reasonable arrangements to have the grievance raised on his behalf by an agent
who unreasonably failed to act, and that Mr Schouten has provided insufficient
evidence of being so affected or traumatised by the matter giving rise to the grievance.
The Authority’s investigation
[6] For the Authority’s investigation, it was agreed that the preliminary matter as to
whether Mr Schouten had exceptional circumstances and should be allowed to pursue
his personal grievance outside the statutory timeframes, should be determined “on the
papers”. Written submissions and documents were lodged by Mr Schouten, and written
submissions were received on behalf of the respondent.
[7] As permitted by s 174E of the Act this determination has stated findings of fact
and law, expressed conclusions on issues necessary to dispose of the matter and
specified orders made. It has not recorded all evidence and submissions received.

The issues
[8] The issues requiring investigation and determination were:
(a) Given that it was accepted that Mr Schouten had raised his personal
grievance outside the timeframes set out in the Act, should leave be
granted by the Authority allowing his personal grievance claim to be
raised and pursued in any event?
(b) Should either party contribute to the costs of representation of the other
party.
Background and supporting documents
[9] Mr Schouten was employed by HNZ as an Orderly. He was dismissed by HNZ
on 7 November 2022.
[10] In an attachment to his statement of problem, Mr Schouten provides a file note
setting out his recollection of events. This note is dated 3 June 2025. In that file note,
Mr Schouten states that in October 2022, he met with a new union representative. He
then “opted out and stopped paying my union fees sometime in early October, mainly
the reason being to do with the cost of living”.
[11] Mr Schouten then states that he “got into contact” with an employment advocate
before the date of his dismissal on 7 November 2022. He states that the advocate “has
been involved in his own way”.
[12] Given the indications by Mr Schouten that there were further pieces of
correspondence about his personal grievance claims, I requested that Mr Schouten
provide to the Authority:
a. a copy of what he said was his personal grievance claim, or any dated
document (including text messages, chat messages, emails or similar)
showing he raised concerns about his dismissal with the respondent; and
b. a copy of any dated document showing that he instructed a
representative or advocate to raise a personal grievance claim on his
behalf within 90 days of his employment ending.

[13] Mr Schouten responded providing further information. He stated that “I had
been in conference with the labour union and was relying on them”. He also stated that
he contacted an employment advocate “to whom I was under the impression of them
being busy working on this matter on my behalf”.
[14] In regard to his correspondence with his union, Mr Schouten provided an email
he had sent to the union dated 9 February 2026, where he stated that he stopped paying
his fees, but a named union representative “stop being in support but was fully informed
of the investigation I was under at that time. Can you please provide me with a letter
that may confirm this chronology. To that the union was in support of helping me with
a personal grievance with my employer the LHDHB [sic]”.
[15] There was a second email in the same string, showing that on 9 February2026,
Mr Schouten’s email had been forwarded to an inbox named “privacyofficer” with the
covering note “Please see the request from ex member Frank Schouten”. Mr Schouten
was copied into this forwarding of this email. The Authority has not received any
further information or correspondence from Mr Schouten in relation to correspondence
with his union.
[16] In regards to his correspondence with the employment advocate, Mr Schouten
provided a one-page written declaration from that advocate, who stated: he advised Mr
Schouten that he would not act for Mr Schouten on a “no win no fee” basis, and that
Mr Schouten did not become one of his clients. The only documents he retained were
a client information sheet completed by Mr Schouten dated on or around 22 November
2022, and “an email forwarded to me by Frank, where he raised a personal grievance
with his employer by way of email on 24 April 2023”. A copy of the client information
sheet which appears to be dated 10 November 2022 was provided. A copy of the
personal grievance email dated 24 April 2023 was not provided. Mr Schouten advised
that there were no further pieces of correspondence to be provided.
Mr Schouten’s submissions
[17] Mr Schouten states that “the chance of pursuing my rights was eliminated by an
advocate whom I relied on during the first 90 days after the termination of employment.
Mr Schouten says he was told “there is nothing you can do about this claim”, and he
relied on this as professional advice at the time. He says “this situation is tantamount
to a special type under 115(b)”.

[18] Mr Schouten further says “one other exceptional circumstance is the loss of
support from the employment trade union”….”I forwarded a letter to the [union] to
advise them to stop my fortnightly union deductions because of the cost of living
situation. There was no further support from the union and I got the feeling of being
abandoned by them.”
[19] Mr Schouten says when he was dismissed, HNZ did not genuinely consider his
explanations, and there is “a manifest, obvious, unjustified dismissal”.
[20] He says that his personal characteristics are important in establishing
exceptional circumstances, being that at the time he was 57 years of age and close to
retirement, that he had always “maintained a sound professional attitude” and a “good
standard of workmanship”, and all of this “caused an unnecessary form of real mental
distress”. He submits that “the law is all about protecting the vulnerable,
underprivileged, and disadvantaged. These factors cumulatively amount to exceptional
circumstances”.
HNZ’s submissions
[21] HNZ submits that none of the circumstances described by Mr Schouten meet
the high threshold for “exceptional circumstances”, or in fact caused the delay between
Mr Schouten’s dismissal and his raising of his personal grievance claim some 2 years
and 8 months later. HNZ submits that in any event, it would not be just to grant leave.
[22] HNZ submits that the information provided by both the employment advocate
and Mr Schouten fall short of showing that Mr Schouten made reasonable arrangements
to have his personal grievance raised on his behalf, and that there are inconsistencies as
to dates in Mr Schouten’s accounts, as well as a lack of certain documents particularly
the alleged personal grievance letter of 24 April 2023. HNZ state that the only personal
grievance claim received by it from Mr Schouten is his application to the Authority
dated 7 July 2025 but received by the Authority on 11 July 2025.
[23] HNZ also submits that the threshold for being so affected or traumatised as to
be unable to raise a personal grievance claim has also not been met. It is submitted that
this is a high threshold, and requires a situation where the affected employee is unable
to properly consider the raising of a grievance for the whole of the 90-day period. HNZ

says that the circumstances Mr Schouten describes simply do not meet this threshold,
and in fact, what he says contradicts this idea, in that he suggests he was relying on
others to act for him.
[24] HNZ says that Mr Schouten has stated that he was advised that his personal
grievance claim was unlikely to be successful, and therefore he accepted that advice
and decided not to pursue matters in a timely way. This does not suggest exceptional
circumstances.
[25] In relation to the union, HNZ states that the delay in raising the grievance was
not caused by any lack of union support, because Mr Schouten’s own evidence is that
he was not a member of the union, and had previously cancelled his membership.
[26] Finally, HNZ submits that it would not be just to grant leave, as the length of
time that has elapsed is sufficient to cause prejudice to it.
[27] In his submissions in reply, Mr Schouten says that “The underlying purpose of
the law of exceptional circumstances is that the law does not protect the situation where
“I know my rights, but fail to exercise them due to reasons from my end”, but covers
innocent people….I was deprived of that knowledge unfairly by an advocate’s view”.
The Employment Relations Act & analysis
[28] Section 114 of the Act requires that a personal grievance must be raised within
the applicable employee notification period, unless the employer consents to the
grievance being raised after this time. The applicable employee notification period in
this case is the period of 90 days beginning with the date on which the action alleged to
amount to a personal grievance occurred or came to the notice of the employee,
whichever is later. In this case, the date the alleged personal grievance occurred is the
date of Mr Schouten’s dismissal.
[29] HNZ does not consent to Mr Schouten raising his personal grievance claim out
of time, therefore Mr Schoten has applied for leave to do so. Section 114(4) of the Act
provides that I may grant leave, if
a. I am satisfied that the delay in raising the personal grievance was
occasioned by exceptional circumstances (which may include any 1 or
more of the circumstances set out in section 115); and

b. I consider it just to do so.
[30] Section 115 of the Act provides that exceptional circumstances include:
a. where the employee has been so affected or traumatised by the matter
giving rise to the grievance that he or she was unable to properly
consider raising the grievance within the applicable employee
notification period under section 114; or
b. where the employee made reasonable arrangements to have the
grievance raised on his or her behalf by an agent of the employee, and
the agent unreasonably failed to ensure that the grievance was raised
within the required time; or
c. where the employee’s employment agreement does not contain the
explanation concerning the resolution of employment relationship
problems that is required by section 54 or section 65, as the case may
be; or
d. where the employer has failed to comply with the obligation under
section 120(1) to provide a statement of reasons for dismissal.
[31] I record that points (c) and (d) do not apply in this case. The applicable
collective agreement contained a compliant dispute resolution provision, and there was
no failure to provide a statement of reasons for dismissal.
[32] Therefore the questions that I need to answer are:
a. was Mr Schouten so affected or traumatised by the dismissal that he was
unable to properly consider raising the grievance within the applicable
period?
b. did Mr Schouten make reasonable arrangements to have the grievance
raised on his or her behalf by an agent of the employee, and the agent
unreasonably failed to ensure that the grievance was raised within the
required time?

[33] Even if one or both of these tests are met, I must also consider if it would be just
to grant leave in the circumstances.
[34] Mr Schouten states that he suffered trauma because at the time of dismissal he
was near retirement age, had been one of the highest regarded staff, and did nothing
wrong. He says “I have been in agony not only from the humiliating termination, but
also for the disappointing conclusion from the advocate and the silence of the union”.
[35] When I consider the information Mr Schouten provided, he states that he
reached out to an employment advocate for assistance a week before his dismissal,
which occurred on 7 November 2022. The client application form provided by him to
the Authority is dated 10 November 2022. Mr Schouten says that he was told by the
advocate that he would not win his case, and/or that the advocate would not act for him
on a no win no fee basis. Having received this information, Mr Schouten said he relied
on it and did not take his case further.
[36] Mr Schouten’s evidence is that he was able to and did consider what steps he
might take to raise a personal grievance both immediately before and shortly after his
termination. Mr Schouten says he received advice from an advocate to the effect that
the advocate did not think his claim was strong, or at the least (according to the
advocate) that the advocate would not act on a no win no fee basis. Although Mr
Schouten is critical of the advocate for not being willing to act for him on a no win no
fee basis, and the evidence of the advocate and the evidence of Mr Schouten are not
completely the same, I find that what this interaction demonstrates is that Mr Schouten
was able to and did, receive initial advice from an advocate and consider his position in
light of that advice. What the evidence shows is that having received some form of
initial advice from the advocate, Mr Schouten decided not to engage the advocate or to
otherwise alter his position.
[37] I find that Mr Schouten was able to properly consider raising a personal
grievance within the applicable employee notification period, and decided not to do so.
Although Mr Schouten states that he suffered from trauma, he states that the trauma
came in part from the dismissal, in part from his disappointment in the actions of the
advocate and in part from his disappointment in a lack of union support. There is no
evidence that the impact on Mr Schouten, at least the part of his trauma that he attributes
to the dismissal as opposed to other matters, was beyond the usual shock experienced

as a result of a dismissal. There is certainly no suggestion that this trauma prevented
Mr Schouten from being able to properly consider raising a personal grievance claim
within time, which the documents show he did so consider, and took some steps toward.
[38] When I stand back and consider this matter, I find that the evidence shows that
Mr Schouten was not so affected or traumatised by the dismissal that he was unable to
properly consider raising the grievance within the applicable period. I find that no
exceptional circumstances exist in relation to the ground set out in s 115(a) of the Act.
[39] I now turn to consider whether Mr Schouten made reasonable arrangements to
have the grievance raised on his or her behalf by an agent of the employee, and the
agent unreasonably failed to ensure that the grievance was raised within the required
time.
[40] Mr Schouten did take some actions to seek advice on his dismissal. He
contacted an employment advocate, and asked if they would assist him to raise a
personal grievance claim on a no win no fee basis.
[41] Mr Schouten says that the advocate did not get back to him for some two-and-
a-half months, and that he was then told that he did not have a high chance of success
and/or that the advocate would not act for him on a no win no fee basis. Mr Schouten
then says he took no further action in reliance on what he was told by the advocate.
[42] It is clear from the information provided by both the advocate and Mr Schouten
that Mr Schouten did make an initial inquiry most likely by filling in a client advice
form on 10 November 2022. It is not clear when the advocate contacted Mr Schouten,
or what the advocate told Mr Schouten, as neither had any records of this. In any event,
what is clear is that Mr Schouten was contacted by the advocate in response to his
inquiry, and as a result of that contact, Mr Schouten decided not to become a client of
the advocate.
[43] Mr Schouten did not take any further steps. Even on his own account, Mr
Schouten never became a client of the advocate, and never issued any instructions to
the advocate requiring the advocate to raise a personal grievance on his behalf.

[44] It is well established that where an employee has instructed an agent to raise a
personal grievance on their behalf, and the agent delays or does not do so, then the
employee should be given some relief because the failure to act was not theirs.
[45] This is not the case here. On Mr Schouten’s own account, I am unable to discern
any arrangements made by him to have the grievance raised on his behalf by an agent.
The agent, that is to say, the employment advocate, did not fail to raise Mr Schouten’s
grievance within time, because they were never instructed by Mr Schouten to raise a
grievance in the first place. In fact, they were never instructed at all, and Mr Schouten
does not claim to have given any such instructions.
[46] Having failed to make any arrangements to have his grievance raised on his
behalf by an agent or advocate, I find that the ground of exceptional circumstances set
out in s 115(b) of the Act does not apply.
[47] I have also considered Mr Schouten’s statement that the union was silent and he
got the feeling that he had been abandoned by them. First, Mr Schouten states multiple
times that prior to his dismissal, he had ceased to be a union member. He does not state
that he contacted the union and asked them to act for him about his dismissal, or to raise
a claim in relation to his dismissal.
[48] I cannot discern why Mr Schouten would expect the union to act on his behalf
when he was no longer a union member, and in circumstances where he is unable to
demonstrate that he contacted them asking them to act on his behalf.
[49] The key point here is that Mr Schouten does not say, and is unable to show, that
he instructed the union to act for him in any way (even if they had an obligation to act
for him in the absence of membership). He also does not say, and is unable to show
that he instructed the union to raise a personal grievance claim on his behalf within the
applicable 90 day period following his dismissal.
[50] In the absence of these arrangements being made by Mr Schouten, the lack of
support from the union cannot amount to exceptional circumstances.
[51] Having found that the matters raised by Mr Schouten do not amount to
exceptional circumstances, I must nevertheless consider whether it would be just to
allow his personal grievance claim to proceed in the circumstances.

[52] Mr Schouten submits that the law relating to exceptional circumstances is to
“cover innocent people” and “I was deprived of that knowledge unfairly by an
advocate’s view” and “I placed my trust in an advocate only to be mislead”.
[53] Having considered all the information provided to me by the parties and Mr
Schouten in particular, I do not agree that this is an accurate reflection of what occurred.
Mr Schouten could have instructed the advocate, or another advocate, lawyer, or his
union, to raise a personal grievance on his behalf. He could also have raised a personal
grievance on his own behalf, as an agent is not required. He did not do so.
[54] Although Mr Schouten has said that he raised a personal grievance at some point
in 2023, he has not provided a copy of this document despite being asked to do so, and
HNZ says it has no record of this. Accordingly, I place no weight on this.
[55] It is apparent that Mr Schouten now wishes to re-visit his earlier decision not to
raise a personal grievance claim, and he is critical of the advocate he chose not to
instruct at the time. His statement of problem touches on this change of position by
stating “I now know I have entitlements under the law” although he does not expand
on this. However, and fundamentally, there is no evidence that Mr Schouten was unable
to raise a personal grievance claim previously. His own evidence is that he investigated
the possibility and chose not to at the relevant time, either by instructing someone else
or by raising a claim on his own behalf.
[56] Having made that decision, and delayed raising his claim for some two years
and eight months, I accept HNZ’s submission that there would be prejudice to it given
the amount of time that has now passed, and the associated difficulties with memory
recall and information retention that this would cause. Overall, I find that it would not
be just to grant leave for the claim to proceed in all the circumstances.
Orders
[57] Having failed to raise a personal grievance within the statutory time frame, no
leave is granted for Mr Schouten to raise his personal grievance claim out of time.
Accordingly, the matter will not progress further.

Costs
[58] Costs are reserved. The parties are encouraged to resolve any issue of costs
between themselves, and I record that my initial view is that no more than the equivalent
of half a day’s tariff would be appropriate.
[59] If the parties are unable to resolve costs, and an Authority determination on
costs is needed, the respondent may lodge, and then should serve, a memorandum on
costs within 28 days of the date of this determination. From the date of service of that
memorandum the applicant will then have 14 days to lodge any reply memorandum.
On request by either party, an extension of time for the parties to continue to negotiate
costs between themselves may be granted.
[60] The parties can anticipate the Authority will determine costs, if asked to do so,
on its usual “daily tariff” basis unless circumstances or factors, require an adjustment
upwards or downwards.1
Claire English
Member of the Employment Relations Authority
1 For further information about the factors considered in assessing costs see:
www.era.govt.nz/determinations/awarding-costs-remedies/#awarding-and-paying-costs-1
